title: Lifting, moving, placing
hookLine: three parts of a step, named softly

cards: Quick question: when your foot leaves the ground, which part leaves first, the heel or the toes? When it comes down, which part lands first? If you have to stand up and check, that's the point.

A movement done countless times stops being felt at all. A step has become one blurry thing: walk. Today's practice slows the blur down until you can see the parts inside it, and gives each part a name.

teach.b: The three-word method comes from Burma, from the teacher Mahasi Sayadaw and his students. Their walking practice uses soft mental labels, called noting. At first you note just: left, right.
As attention sharpens, you break each step into parts.
Lifting: the heel rises, the foot comes up. Moving: the foot swings forward through the air. Placing: the foot comes down and touches the ground.
You say the words silently, lightly, at the same moment as the movement. Not before, not after. The labels are like a flashlight, keeping attention on exactly what's happening.

teach.h: A STEP IS NOT ONE THING.
teach.b: Slow down this much and people discover that a step is not one thing. Lifting has its own feel, a lightness. Moving has a floating quality.
Placing has the pressure, the contact, the weight coming back. Each part begins and ends: the impermanence you met in the breath, now in your feet. Taking a step apart isn't new.

teach.h: SIX PARTS IN THE OLD MANUAL.
teach.b: The Visuddhimagga, the old manual you met with counting, analyzes a single step into six parts, from lifting through to pressing down, and says each part arises and passes away in its own moment.

Mahasi's three labels are a simpler doorway into the same observation. Some teachers use noting; others, in the Thai forest tradition for instance, simply feel the steps without words, or use a quiet word like Buddho.
Different schools, the same attention. And it's slow, much slower than feels normal. That's fine.

how: In the Burmese noting tradition of Mahasi Sayadaw, meditators walk slowly, silently labeling each part of the step, lifting, moving, placing; other traditions walk with attention but without labels.

games.q: you're noting your steps and realize you said placing before your foot touched down. what do you do?
o: walk faster so the words keep up.
slow down so the word matches the movement.
games.why: the label goes with the movement, not before or after: slow down until they match.

practice: Stand at one end of your lane, or any few paces of floor, feel the weight in both feet, and begin very slowly: as the heel rises, silently, lifting; as the foot travels forward, moving; as it touches down, placing; then the other foot.

Keep the words soft, a whisper in the mind matching the movement exactly, and if the mind wanders, stop, stand, feel the feet, and begin again. If you can't stand, lift and place one foot while seated.
